title: Call stacks and debugging an error in production

videos.script: Lesson 36 left a server alive after a panic, with a stack trace in its log. This lesson is about reading that trace, and about the program that printed it. {{trace}} First, a bug three calls deep. The trace lists the functions that were running, deepest first, each with a file and a line. You will read it one frame at a time, including the frames the compiler folded into their callers. {{context}} Then, how to get more out of a failure. An environment variable decides how much the runtime prints. And a recover at a boundary can write the trace itself, beside a structured log line, while the program carries on. {{production}} Last, the question every incident starts with: which code is this? A Go binary carries its module version, its commit and the Go that built it, and the program can read them about itself. You will also see what trimpath and stripping take out of a binary, and that the file and the line survive both. By the end, a trace from a machine you have never logged into is enough to find the line that broke.
